subject: philosophy
title: Argument Fundamentals
objective: Put a claim, its reasons, a counterexample, and a repair together.

lesson.opening: This is an original practical argument, not a quotation from a historical thinker. You will test a proposed museum policy using the tools of World 0. Treat understanding the policy and endorsing it as separate tasks.

sections.heading: A complete examination
sections.body:
A museum proposes displaying every donated object. Its supporter argues that displaying gifts respects donors, and that respecting donors is always the right policy. Before voting on the proposal, reconstruct the argument. Identify what the reasons establish, where a universal claim enters, and what additional considerations might matter.

An objection should target a claim or an inference. A fragile object may be destroyed by exposure to light; an object may also have been donated by someone without a rightful claim to it. These are different objections. The first concerns preservation, the second rightful possession. A repair that answers one does not automatically answer the other.

In this boss, aim to understand and improve an argument rather than defeat a person. A principled revision should apply to future cases, not merely exempt the one difficult object mentioned today. You can oppose or support the policy while giving an accurate reconstruction.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the argument
sections.body: The argument moves from displaying donations to respecting donors, then from donor respect to right policy. It needs a bridge from a policy being right to our implementing it. The manuscript introduces a competing obligation of preservation.

sections.heading: A serious objection
sections.body: A donor says that withholding an object from display betrays the gift’s purpose. A serious reply must explain how preservation can honor that purpose over time, or why the purpose does not settle the institution’s duties.

activities.prompt: Which statement supplies the broad normative premise?
choices: Every policy that respects donors is right.

activities.prompt: A policy pleases donors by destroying irreplaceable evidence. If that policy is wrong, it is…
choices: A counterexample to the claim that all donor-respecting policies are right.
Evidence that all museums are unjust.
Display everything except this one named manuscript.
Provide access consistent with preservation and rightful possession, explaining restrictions to donors.

activities.prompt: Which reply addresses the donor’s objection?
choices: Preserving the manuscript can sustain future access, which may better serve the gift’s educational purpose.

activities.prompt: If the original argument’s form is valid but its donor-respect premise is false, it is…
choices: Neither an argument nor a policy.

activities.prompt: Which evidence would best support an inductive claim that protective restrictions improve long-term access?
choices: A representative comparison of preservation outcomes across comparable collections.

activities.prompt: Reconstruct the original policy argument, identify a serious objection, and defend a principled revision. You may also reject universal display entirely.
activities.context: Every donated object should be displayed, because displaying donations respects donors, and every policy that respects donors is right. A newly donated manuscript will be irreversibly damaged by prolonged exposure to light.
rubric: I identify the normative premise and conclusion.
I explain exactly which premise or inference my objection targets.
My revision addresses the objection and applies beyond one case.
